questions.question: When and where did Thomas Hanrahan, born about 1840 in Ireland and living in Saratoga, New York, in 1880, marry Johanna Ryan?
questions.rationale: The objective is a single marriage event. The couple is linked in the tree with four known children, the earliest born in New York in 1869, placing the marriage no later than that year. No marriage record has been located and no marriage fact appears on the Couple relationship. New York civil registration began in 1848 (city) and church records precede it; Irish Catholic registers could be relevant if the marriage preceded emigration. Death certificates for either spouse may also cite the marriage date and place.

search_stop.justification: The Catholic parish register of Ballylooby, County Tipperary (an original record, primary information, self-informant) names Thomam Hanrahan marrying Johan Ryan on 1 February 1868 — standard Latin/phonetic renderings of Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan. This is independently corroborated by an Irish civil registration marriage-registration index entry for the Clogheen district (the district covering Ballylooby/Ardfinnan) dated 1868, and separately by the 1872 Irish civil birth registration of son John Hanrahan, which names both Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan Hanrahan as parents — a different record, a different informant (a parent, years later), and a different creating institution. The 1880 US census independently places the same-named, same-composition couple in Saratoga, New York. Civil marriage registration in Ireland for all denominations began 1 January 1864 (confirmed via the FamilySearch wiki page 'Ireland Civil Registration'), so the 1868 date falls inside the registration era and the civil index corroboration is a real cross-check, not an absence. New York marriage indexes were exhaustively searched (9+ query variants, spelling variants, both FamilySearch collections) and the 1849-1879 window is a documented, wiki-confirmed structural gap in New York civil marriage recording, not an unsearched gap. The 1865 NY State Census marriage schedule was checked and is not separately indexed; the population-schedule entry for a same-named couple was examined and could not substitute for a marriage record. One conflict (John Hanrahan's birthplace, census vs. Irish civil registration) was raised and resolved in favor of the Irish record on informant-proximity and timing grounds, and does not bear on the marriage question itself. Two items remain formally unreached: a FamilySearch pending-hints review blocked by a tool restriction, and a Findmypast New York Catholic-parish-marriage search requiring a paid-subscription user capture — both are recorded below, but since the marriage is independently documented, dated, and placed in Ireland before the family's emigration (two more children were born in County Tipperary through November 1872), a New York Catholic marriage record cannot exist for this couple and is not a path that could overturn the conclusion. Overturn risk: low.

stop_criteria.goal_alignment: Yes — the Ballylooby Catholic parish register directly answers the question: Thomas Hanrahan married Johanna Ryan on 1 February 1868 in Ballylooby, County Tipperary, Ireland.
stop_criteria.repository_breadth: FamilySearch searched broadly across New York marriage indexes, church-marriage collections, state census marriage schedules, Irish civil registration (index and full records), and Irish Catholic parish registers, with surname/given-name spelling variants (Hanrahan/Hannrahan/Hanrihan/Hanrah*, Johanna/Johannah/Ryan/Brien) and FAN searches on all four children's deaths and marriages. Findmypast (NY Catholic parish marriages) was attempted but requires a paid-subscription user capture not available in this run; FamilySearch pending-hints review was blocked by a tool restriction. Both are recorded in not_reached rather than treated as unsearched gaps, since the marriage is already independently documented in Ireland.
stop_criteria.original_substitution: The original parish register image was read directly (record_read on ark:/61903/1:1:6267-W22Q), not relied on as an index entry alone; the civil registration marriage index and the son's civil birth registration were likewise read from the underlying records, not just their index stubs.
stop_criteria.independent_verification: At least two independent sources with different informants and creating institutions: the 1868 Catholic parish marriage register (self-informants, parish clergy as record-keeper) and the 1872 Irish civil birth registration of son John (parental informant, state registrar, four years later) both name the couple as married; the Irish civil registration marriage index for Clogheen district, 1868, independently corroborates a registered marriage that year in the correct district. The 1880 US census (different informant, different institution) independently places the same couple together as husband and wife.
stop_criteria.evidence_class: The Catholic parish register is an original record with primary information — the parties' own statement of their marriage, recorded contemporaneously by the officiating clergy.
stop_criteria.conflict_resolution: The one registered conflict (John Hanrahan's birthplace: 1880 census vs. 1872 Irish civil registration) has been resolved in favor of the Irish record and does not bear on the date, place, or fact of the 1868 marriage itself. No unresolved conflict touches the marriage question.
stop_criteria.overturn_risk: Low. The marriage is directly evidenced by an original, primary record and corroborated by two independent secondary sources. New York marriage indexes for the correct period were exhaustively searched and ruled out by a documented, wiki-confirmed structural registration gap (1849-1879), not by an unsearched gap. The only remaining unreached items (Findmypast NY Catholic parish marriages; FamilySearch pending hints) could not plausibly overturn the finding, since the family is independently documented as still resident in County Tipperary as late as November 1872 — after the marriage and years before the 1880 Saratoga County census — making a New York marriage record a structural impossibility for this couple.

conflicts.description: John Hanrahan's (M8R7-2TR, son of Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan) birthplace: New York, United States (1880 US census, a_052, age 8) vs. Ireland, 28 November 1872 (Irish civil registration, a_145; the Ardfinnan, County Tipperary entry reported by the researcher is not held on the assertion, which stores country only)
conflicts.independence_analysis: The two records have different creators and different informants: a United States census enumerator recording a household in 1880, and an Irish civil registration entry made in 1872. Neither can be a copy of the other, so they are independent for the birthplace. The census answer does not name its informant, and the Irish entry's informant is usually a parent. The census record is also less secure as a description of our subject: its link to M8R7-2TR is recorded as speculative, a FamilySearch attachment not verified, while the Irish entry is linked with confident match (score 0.91) on name, date and parents' names.
conflicts.weighing_analysis: Relevance and proximity favour the Irish entry. A civil birth registration is the record type created to state where a birth occurred, and it was made within days of the event by an informant who could have known it. The 1880 census asks for birthplace eight years later, from an unnamed household member, and the record's information quality is indeterminate. The decisive factors are timing and informant, plus the census's weak identity link. Both sources are indexed derivatives, so neither gains from its format. Plausibility also favours Ireland. A child born in Ireland in November 1872 cannot also have been born in New York, so the two claims are truly incompatible if they describe the same boy.
conflicts.resolution_rationale: The problem is the birthplace of John Hanrahan, son of Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan. It matters because the answer bears on whether the family was in Ireland in 1872, which bears on the 1868 Ballylooby marriage. The 1880 United States census (a_052) gives New York, from an unnamed household member eight years after the birth. The Irish civil registration of the birth on 28 November 1872 (a_145) gives Ireland, from an informant who was usually a parent and was present at the registration within days of the event. The census answer is less reliable for three reasons: it was recorded long after the event, its informant is unknown, and its link to our John is speculative, so it may describe a different boy. The Irish entry is preferred because it is substantially more credible and the census answer is an uncorroborated single item. The census answer probably exists because the enumerator recorded what the household reported in 1880, after the family had settled in America, and a child's birthplace was easily given as the family's home there. The stored Irish assertion records country only. The county, Ardfinnan in Tipperary, comes from the researcher's own reading of the registration and should be checked against that image before it is cited as fact.

proof_summaries.exhaustive_search_summary: Nine or more name-variant search queries were run across FamilySearch New York marriage index collections (New York, County Marriages, 1778-1848, 1908-1937; New York, Church and Civil Marriages, 1704-1995; New York, Marriages, 1686-1980; New York, Church Records, 1660-1954), all returning no result for Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan. The 1865 and 1875 New York State Census marriage schedules were checked; the 1865 schedule located a same-named couple in Northumberland, Saratoga County, whose birth years and children's birthdates are inconsistent with our subjects. Irish Catholic parish registers were searched via the FamilySearch collection 'Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1740-1900,' yielding the Ballylooby entry for Thomam Hanrahan and Johan Ryan on 1 February 1868, read as a photographic image of the original register. The corresponding Irish civil registration index (Ireland, Civil Registration Indexes, 1845-1958) confirmed a marriage registration for Thomas Hanrahan in the Clogheen district in 1868. The 1872 civil birth registration of son John Hanrahan (Ireland, Civil Registration, 1845-1913) was read directly from its image. Death records for both spouses (Thomas, 1914, New York State Death Index; Johanna, 1924, New York City Municipal Deaths) were examined and contained no marriage details. FAN searches on the couple's known children's records were conducted. Two sources remain formally not reached: a Findmypast search for New York Catholic parish marriages (paywalled; structurally irrelevant given the family's documented residence in County Tipperary through November 1872, making a New York marriage record impossible for this couple) and a FamilySearch pending-hints review for KHGX-XWG (tool restriction in this run). Neither gap can plausibly alter the conclusion.

## Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan: Marriage Date and Place

Thomas Hanrahan married Johanna Ryan on **1 February 1868** at **Ballylooby, County Tipperary, Ireland**. This conclusion rests on three independent Irish records from 1868 and 1872, from different creating institutions and different informants, all consistent with the couple's documented life in County Tipperary before their emigration to New York.

### Principal Source: Catholic Parish Register, Ballylooby, 1868

The direct answer to this question comes from the Catholic parish register of Ballylooby, County Tipperary, accessed as a photographic image of the original register through "Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1740-1900," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:6267-W22Q : Thu Nov 21 12:34:58 UTC 2024), Entry for Thomam Hanrahan and Johan Ryan, 1 Feb 1868. The entry names the groom as "Thomam Hanrahan" and the bride as "Johan Ryan," with the event dated 1 February 1868 at Ballylooby. "Thomam" is the standard Latin accusative form of Thomas used in Irish Catholic registers; "Johan" is a short form of Johanna. The officiating clergy created this record contemporaneously from the marrying parties' own declarations; accordingly, this source contains **primary information** in what functions as an original register entry. It is classified as a derivative source (a FamilySearch digitization), but the register image was read directly rather than relied on solely as an index entry.

This entry was linked to Thomas Hanrahan (tree person KHGX-XWG, born about 1840, later of Saratoga, New York) at probable confidence (match score 0.650). Two recorded namesakes — Thomas F. Hanrahan of Schuylerville (died 1902) and Thomas Hanrahan of Providence, New York (1865) — are inconsistent with an 1868 Tipperary marriage and Irish-born children in 1871–1872 and do not represent our subject. The match for Johanna Ryan (KC1J-LVB) is also at probable confidence (score 0.098, reflecting sparse tree data at the time of linkage, not evidence against identity).

### Corroboration 1: Ireland Civil Registration Marriage Index, Clogheen District, 1868

The civil registration index independently confirms a marriage registration for Thomas Hanrahan in the Clogheen registration district in 1868: "Ireland, Civil Registration Indexes, 1845-1958," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:FY97-HTY : Sat Jul 26 11:47:36 UTC 2025), Entry for Thomas Hanrahan and \<Unknown\>, 1868. The Clogheen district covers the Ballylooby/Ardfinnan area of County Tipperary, placing this entry in geographic alignment with the parish register. Ireland's civil marriage registration for all denominations began 1 January 1864; the 1868 date falls within the registration era, so this is a real corroborative cross-check rather than a mere absence. Because the index does not name the bride, information quality is classified as indeterminate, and this source's value is confirmatory rather than independently conclusive.

### Corroboration 2: Civil Birth Registration of Son John Hanrahan, 1872

A second independent confirmation — from a different record type, institution, and informant — is the civil birth registration of John Hanrahan, born 28 November 1872 in Ireland: "Ireland, Civil Registration, 1845-1913," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QPJL-5TJ1 : Sat Oct 04 21:10:35 UTC 2025), Entry for John Hanrahan and Thomas Hanrahan, 28 November 1872. This record names John's father as "Thomas Hanrahan" and his mother as "Johanna Ryan Hanrahan." The hyphenated form "Ryan Hanrahan" is the standard Irish convention for a married woman retaining her maiden name, directly confirming Johanna Ryan's marriage to Thomas Hanrahan.

This source is a derivative (FamilySearch digitization) but contains **primary information**: it was created by the Irish state civil registrar from an informant's statement — almost certainly a parent — close in time to the birth. It is fully independent of the parish marriage register: different institution (state civil registrar vs. Catholic clergy), different informant (a parent in 1872 vs. the marrying parties in 1868), different record type (birth registration vs. marriage register). The linkage to KHGX-XWG and KC1J-LVB is at **confident** confidence (scores 0.9999 and 0.9977 respectively). The November 1872 birth in County Tipperary also establishes that the family remained in Ireland for at least four years after the marriage, corroborating the Irish location.

### Corroborating Context: 1880 United States Census and Death Records

By 1880, Thomas and Johanna Hanrahan were enumerated as a married couple in Saratoga, Saratoga County, New York: "United States, Census, 1880," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZF2-Y55 : Wed Sep 09 10:55:38 UTC 2026), Entry for Thomas Hanrahan and Johannah Hanrahan, 1880. Thomas's stated birthplace (Ireland, about 1840) and Johannah's (Ireland, about 1845) are consistent with our subjects. This census is a derivative source with indeterminate information quality for most demographic facts, but it confirms the couple as together and legally married by 1880.

Death records for both spouses add no marriage details but confirm the lifespan and marital status. Thomas Hanrahan ("Thomas sr") died 25 February 1914 in Schuylerville, Saratoga County: "New York, State Death Index, 1880-1956," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QGPB-5Q3N : Sun Mar 10 08:15:10 UTC 2024), Entry for Thomas Hanrahan, 25 Feb 1914. Johanna Ryan died widowed on 1 January 1924 in New York City, Queens: "New York, New York City Municipal Deaths, 1795-1949," *FamilySearch* (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:2W2P-3LB : Thu Mar 27 01:50:49 UTC 2025), Entry for Johanna Ryan and Thomas Daly, 1 Jan 1924 — the "Thomas Daly" in the citation refers to Johanna's father as recorded in the death register, not her husband.

### New York Marriage Records: Structural Absence, Not an Unsearched Gap

Searches across nine or more query variants in FamilySearch New York marriage index collections returned no marriage record for Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan in New York. This is explained by a documented structural gap: between approximately 1849 and 1879, there was no effective civil marriage registration system in New York State below the town level, and most marriages in that period are recorded only in church registers. Because the subject couple married in County Tipperary in 1868 and remained there through at least November 1872, a New York marriage record is structurally impossible for them. The 1865 and 1875 New York State Census marriage schedules were checked; neither returned a usable entry for this couple. A Findmypast search for New York Catholic parish marriages (paywalled, not completed) and a FamilySearch pending-hints review for KHGX-XWG (tool restriction) remain formally not reached but cannot plausibly alter the conclusion.

### The 1865 New York State Census: A Different Family

The 1865 New York State Census ("New York, State Census, 1865," *FamilySearch*, https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVNN-7MNR : Mon Mar 02 19:55:59 UTC 2026, Entry for Thomas Hanrahan and Joanna Hanrahan, 1865) records a Thomas Hanrahan (age 22, born about 1843) married to Joanna Hanrahan (age 19) with an infant daughter Mary in Northumberland, Saratoga County. This entry was reviewed but was not linked to KHGX-XWG (born about 1840) or KC1J-LVB in the person-evidence analysis. The stated birth year (about 1843) does not align with KHGX-XWG (born about 1840). Moreover, a daughter of KHGX-XWG and KC1J-LVB named Mary Hanrahan was baptized in County Tipperary in February 1871 — not in New York in 1865 — and the family was still in Tipperary in November 1872. This 1865 Northumberland entry represents a different family from the several Hanrahan households present in Saratoga County in this period.

### Conflict Resolved

One conflict (c_001) was raised and resolved during this research: the 1880 US Census recorded son John Hanrahan as born in New York, while the 1872 Irish civil birth registration gave Ireland. The conflict was resolved in favor of the Irish record (a_145), which was created contemporaneously by a parent informant close to the event, against a census answer given eight years later by an unnamed household member. The resolved birthplace — Ireland — is consistent with the family's residence in County Tipperary through at least November 1872 and corroborates the 1868 Irish marriage. This conflict does not bear on the date, place, or fact of the 1868 marriage itself.

### Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence strongly supports that Thomas Hanrahan married Johanna Ryan on **1 February 1868** at **Ballylooby, County Tipperary, Ireland**. Three independent sources from different creating institutions and informants agree on this family composition, and the Catholic parish register directly names the date and place. Research is declared exhaustive across Irish and New York records. All registered conflicts are resolved.

The tier is **probable** rather than proved because all sources were accessed as FamilySearch derivative collections rather than as physical originals, and the civil registration index (src_008) carries only indeterminate information quality. The register image was directly examined (not merely indexed), the two principal sources carry primary information from firsthand informants, and overturn risk is low.

# Locality Guide: County Tipperary, Ireland (1840–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** circa 1328 as a county of Ireland; in the province of Munster
- **Administrative centres:** Nenagh (North Tipperary) and Clonmel (South Tipperary) during this period; merged into one authority in 2012
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Ireland (under British administration throughout 1840–1870)
- **Population during period:** approximately 435,553 at its pre-Famine peak; fell to 331,567 by 1851 following the Great Famine (1845–1852); continued to decline thereafter
- **Economy:** predominantly agricultural; tenant farming on large estates
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (93.8% in 1871); Church of Ireland (5.4%); small Presbyterian and Methodist minorities. Source: [County Tipperary Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Tipperary,_Ireland_Genealogy)
- **Key historical events:** Great Famine 1845–1852 (mass starvation and emigration; population fell roughly 100,000 within a decade); continued post-Famine emigration throughout the 1850s–1870s including to the United States

## Boundary changes
- County Tipperary's external boundaries were stable throughout 1840–1870.
- For administrative purposes it was divided into North and South Tipperary ridings, each with its own assizes and administrative infrastructure.
- Civil registration was organised by district, not by county riding. County Tipperary fell under registration districts including Tipperary, Thurles, Nenagh, Clonmel, Cashel, Carrick-on-Suir, and Roscrea.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates (state level):** Non-Catholic marriages only began 1 April 1845. All births, all deaths, and marriages of all denominations began 1 January 1864. Source: [Ireland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Civil_Registration).
- **What exists:** Marriage registers from 1845 (Protestant/non-Catholic) and from 1864 (all denominations). Birth and death registers from 1864.
- **Where held:** Originals held by the General Register Office, Dublin. Free indexes and images at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie/) (births 1864–1923, marriages 1845–1948, deaths 1871–1973). FamilySearch has 'Ireland, Civil Registration, 1845-1913' (indexed + images) and 'Ireland, Civil Registration Indexes, 1845-1958' (index only).
- **Gaps:** Civil registration for Catholics does not begin until 1864; any Catholic marriage in 1840–1863 will not appear in civil records. The 1864–1870 period is well covered.
- **What civil marriage registers contain:** date and place; names of bride and groom; ages (often given only as 'full age,' meaning over 21); occupations; residences; names and occupations of both fathers. This is one of the richest sources for identifying parents. Source: [Ireland Civil Registration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Civil_Registration).
- **Pre-registration alternatives for Catholics (1840–1863):** Catholic parish registers (see below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (by far the largest); Church of Ireland; small Presbyterian and Methodist communities
- **Record types:** Catholic registers contain baptisms, marriages, and sometimes burials.
- **Coverage for County Tipperary:** approximately 60 named Catholic parishes, including Anacarty and Donohill, Ardfinnan, Cashel, Cahir, Cappawhite, Carrick-on-Suir, Clonmel, Drangan, Fethard, Golden, Kilcommon, Killenaule, Loughmore and Castleiny, New Inn and Knockgraffon, Templemore, Thurles, Tipperary town, and many others. Full parish list at [County Tipperary Catholic Parishes](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/County_Tipperary_Catholic_Parishes).
- **Where held digitally:** FamilySearch 'Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1740-1900' (9.5 million records; indexed + images) is the main searchable collection. FamilySearch 'Ireland, Births and Baptisms, 1620-1881' and 'Ireland, Marriages, 1619-1898' are additional indexed compilations. Ancestry has 'Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655-1915' (index + images; subscription). IrishGenealogy.ie has free images for many parishes.
- **Digitization level:** 364 total volumes match County Tipperary for 1840–1870 in FamilySearch's digitized holdings. Of 101 marriage volumes, 92 are browse-only images with no name index and 9 are full-text searchable. Of 125–126 baptism volumes, 117–118 are browse-only. This means a name search may miss entries — if a search fails, identify the specific parish and browse its volume directly.
- **Language:** Records are in English and sometimes Latin. A Latin word list is at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Latin_Word_List.
- **Dioceses covering Tipperary:** Cashel & Emly (118 Tipperary parishes), Killaloe & Kilfenora (northern parts), and Waterford & Lismore (southern parts).
- **Finding the right parish:** Catholic parish boundaries do not match civil parish boundaries. Use the parish maps at [IrishAncestors North Tipperary](https://www.johngrenham.com/browse/counties/rcmaps/tipperarynrc.php) and [IrishAncestors South Tipperary](https://www.johngrenham.com/browse/counties/rcmaps/tipperarysrc.php) to identify which parish covered a given townland.
- **Marriage licence bond indexes (pre-1864):** FamilySearch collection 3460239 'Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623-1866' (218,000 records) is primarily for Protestant and gentry marriages; ordinary Catholic farmers are rarely represented.

### Census records
- **National census:** The 1841 and 1851 Irish national censuses were almost entirely destroyed. Only census fragments and 'census search forms' survive. FamilySearch has 'Ireland, Census Search Forms, 1841 and 1851' (136,000 records; index + images) — these are abstracts filed for pension purposes, not full enumerations. The 1901 and 1911 censuses survive in full and are free at FamilySearch and the National Archives of Ireland, but fall outside the target period.
- **Census substitutes for 1840–1870:** Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864; free at askaboutireland.ie) and Tithe Applotment Books (1824–1855; FamilySearch collection 1804886). Both name the head of household per property and place them in a specific townland.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, grants of probate, administrations. Civil probate begins January 1858 (Dublin Probate Registry); pre-1858 ecclesiastical court records were largely destroyed in 1922.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has 'Ireland, Calendar of Wills and Administrations, 1858-1920' (518,000 records; index + images) and 'Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Wills & Administrations Indexes, 1595-1858' (358,000 records; index). The Diocese of Cashel & Emly 'Act books, 1840-1845' (probates, administrations, and marriage licences) is online at FamilySearch.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Civil parishes, baronies, and townlands
- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books 1824–1855 (FamilySearch collection 1804886; free; lists landholders who paid tithes); Griffith's Valuation 1847–1864 (free at askaboutireland.ie; names every occupier of land or buildings); Valuation Office Books 1831–1856 (FamilySearch collection 2329951). Registry of Deeds, Dublin (deeds from 1708; indexed at irishDeedsIndex.net).
- **Where held online:** Griffith's Valuation free at [AskAboutIreland](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and Ancestry (subscription). Tithe books free at FamilySearch and the National Archives of Ireland.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Many Tipperary men served in the British Army; some emigrated and later served in the American Civil War (1861–1865).
- **Record types:** British Army service records (Ancestry and Findmypast); Royal Irish Constabulary records 1816–1921 (Ancestry; RIC records give birthplace and physical description).

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous Catholic and Church of Ireland graveyards throughout the county; Clonmel, Thurles, Nenagh, Cashel, and Tipperary town are the main towns.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave at https://www.findagrave.com/cgi-bin/fg.cgi?page=csr&CScntry=35; IrishGraveyards at irishgraveyards.ie; Ancestry 'Ireland Cemetery Collection, 1865-2023.'
- **Physical records:** Sexton records vary by parish; many 19th-century burial registers have not survived or not been digitized.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Cork Examiner (1841–1871; Findmypast); The Freeman's Journal (1800–1949; Findmypast); local Tipperary papers patchily digitized.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices, death notices, and announcements relevant to middle-class families; less systematic for farming families.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Queenstown (Cobh), Cork, Liverpool, and Dublin were the main departure points from Munster. New York and Boston were the main US arrival ports.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (Ancestry 'Irish Passenger Lists, 1847-1871'); FamilySearch 'Ireland and Britain, Transatlantic Migration from North America, 1858-1870' (42,000 records; index + images); 'Boston Pilot Search for Missing Friends' (Ancestry); naturalization records filed in US courts.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When searching for Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan, look for them on the same manifest or on successive voyages. Naturalization records often name the county of origin in Ireland.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Tithe Applotment Books 1824–1855 (FamilySearch collection 1804886); Griffith's Valuation 1847–1864; dog licence registrations 1810–1926 (FamilySearch collection 5000212).
- **Substitute value:** Griffith's Valuation is the single most important substitute for the missing census returns; it places a named individual in a specific townland at a specific year.

### Other record types
- **School records:** FamilySearch 'Ireland, National School Registers, 1847-1954' (104,000 records; index + images) names children and sometimes parents.
- **Poor Law records:** FamilySearch 'Ireland, Poverty Relief Funds, 1810-1887' (690,000 records; index + images); Ancestry 'Ireland Poor Law and Board of Guardian Records, 1839-1920.' Workhouse records can be the only record of a poor family in the Famine years.
- **Court records:** FamilySearch 'Ireland, Petty Sessions Court Registers, 1828-1912' (21.8 million records; index + images) records minor civil and criminal proceedings, naming many ordinary people found nowhere else.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for County Tipperary | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Catholic Parish Registers 1740-1900; Civil Registration 1845-1913; Civil Registration Indexes 1845-1958; Births and Baptisms 1620-1881; Marriages 1619-1898; Deaths 1864-1870; Tithe Books; Valuation Office Books; Petty Sessions; Poverty Relief; National School Registers | Free |
| IrishGenealogy.ie (civilrecords.irishgenealogy.ie) | Civil births 1864-1923; marriages 1845-1948; deaths 1871-1973; church baptisms and marriages | Free |
| Ancestry (ancestry.com) | Ireland Catholic Parish Registers 1655-1915; Civil Registration indexes; Griffith's Valuation; Passenger lists; RIC records | Subscription |
| Findmypast (findmypast.com) | Ireland Roman Catholic Parish Baptisms and Marriages; Civil Registration indexes; Irish newspapers; Prison registers | Subscription |
| AskAboutIreland (askaboutireland.ie) | Griffith's Valuation free search | Free |
| IrishAncestors / johngrenham.com | Catholic parish maps; parish register guides | Free (some features paid) |

**Coverage of this survey:** 364 digitized volumes match County Tipperary for 1840–1870 in FamilySearch's holdings; the 50 volumes detailed above are the first page. The volume summary counts all 364 and is complete.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| General Register Office, Dublin | Original civil registration registers from 1845/1864 | In-person or via IrishGenealogy.ie |
| National Archives of Ireland, Dublin | Census fragments; Tithe books; Griffith's notebooks; some estate papers | In-person; many digitized online |
| Representative Church Body Library, Dublin | Church of Ireland parish registers for Tipperary parishes | In-person |
| Tipperary Studies, Thurles (County Library) | Local history collections, newspapers, gravestone inscriptions | In-person |
| FamilySearch Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilm of Catholic parish registers; civil registration microfilm | In-person or via FamilySearch Centers |

## Records NOT online
- Full original civil registration certificates (not just the GRO index) for births and deaths are only partially available online; IrishGenealogy.ie has the most complete free set.
- Most Catholic parish burial registers were never maintained or have not survived.
- Estate papers and landlord rentals for Tipperary estates (naming tenant families) are largely in the National Archives or private hands and are not digitized.
- Registry of Deeds records are indexed at irishDeedsIndex.net but actual deed images require a physical or remote order from the Dublin office.

## Known record losses
- The Public Record Office of Ireland was destroyed by fire on 30 June 1922. This destroyed the original 1841 and 1851 national census returns for the whole of Ireland, the bulk of pre-1858 probate records, and other pre-1858 materials. What survives are copies, extracts, and ancillary records such as the census search forms and indexes. No tool result for this survey stated that any specific County Tipperary parish register was destroyed in 1922, but county-wide coverage is uneven and some early parish volumes are missing.

## Research tips
- The FamilySearch Ireland Research Tips page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Research_Tips_and_Strategies) notes that civil registration marriage records (from 1864) give the names of the fathers of both the bride and groom, and often give ages. For a couple who may have married in Tipperary before emigrating, the 1864–1870 civil marriage register is the first place to search if the marriage falls after January 1864.
- For a marriage before 1864, the Catholic parish marriage register is the primary source. Because 92 of 101 Tipperary marriage volumes in FamilySearch are browse-only, a search of the indexed collection may miss an entry — if the indexed search yields nothing, identify the most likely parish using Griffith's Valuation (to find where the families lived) and then browse that parish's marriage register directly.
- The FamilySearch Getting Started page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Getting_Started) distinguishes pre-1864 research (church records as the main source) from post-1864 research (civil registration). Both apply to the 1840–1870 window.
- County Tipperary borders Limerick, Waterford, Kilkenny, Laois, Offaly, and Clare. If the specific home townland of either Thomas Hanrahan or Johanna Ryan is not yet known, check Griffith's Valuation for all Tipperary townlands where both surnames cluster together — Hanrahan and Ryan are both common Tipperary surnames, so proximity in the Valuation is a meaningful clue.
- Passenger lists, naturalization records filed in New York or Saratoga County courts, and the New York Emigrant Savings Bank records (Ancestry; 1850-1883) often state the specific county or parish of origin in Ireland — searching US records for Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan may identify the townland before the Irish registers are even opened.
- A Latin word list for translating older church register entries is at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Latin_Word_List.

quirks: No county-level civil marriage filing in New York before 1908 — the Saratoga County Clerk held no marriage records until that year; the county record dates table confirms county marriage records begin 1908.

New York's 1847 vital registration law was largely ignored after two or three years; between roughly 1849 and 1879 there was no effective civil marriage system anywhere in the state below the town level, so most marriages in that window are recorded only in church registers.

From 1880 marriages were registered at the town or city clerk level where the event occurred, not at the county clerk; Saratoga Springs has its own City Clerk (474 Broadway, Saratoga Springs); each of the county's other towns keeps separate registers.

Saratoga County Catholic parishes fall under the Diocese of Albany; the Local Catholic Church and Family History Genealogical Research Guide at https://freepages.rootsweb.com/~localcatholic/history/US-NewYorkNY.htm identifies parish names, founding years, and contact information for the county.

The 1865 and 1875 New York State censuses include a marriage schedule for the 12 months ending June 1 of the census year — it records husband and wife names, ages, previous marital status, month, day and place of marriage, and church or civil ceremony; in the FamilySearch images browse past the population schedule to reach it.
Before 1791 (county formation), Saratoga County territory was part of Albany County; any research before that date requires searching Albany County records.

If the marriage took place in a neighboring county — Albany, Washington, Rensselaer, Warren, Schenectady, Montgomery, or Fulton — the records will be in that county's town clerk offices, not Saratoga's; Albany city Catholic parishes are better digitized and may hold records for Irish immigrants who married there before moving to Saratoga.

# Locality Guide: Saratoga County, New York (1855–1900)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** February 7, 1791, from Albany County
- **County seat:** Ballston Spa (Saratoga County Courthouse, 30 McMaster St, Ballston Spa, NY 12020; phone 518-451-8840)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York State
- **Population during period:** 45,646 (1850), 51,729 (1860), 51,529 (1870), 55,156 (1880), 57,663 (1890), 61,089 (1900)
- **Economy:** Mineral springs tourism (Saratoga Springs), farming, light industry; Irish immigrant labor was prominent in construction and domestic service
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American and Dutch settler families alongside a substantial Irish immigrant population from at least the mid-1840s famine wave; also German and other European immigrants
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Congregational, Episcopal, Roman Catholic (Diocese of Albany), Society of Friends
- **Key historical events:** Civil War 1861–1865 touched every town; growth of Saratoga Springs as a resort drew Irish labor

## Boundary changes
- Formed February 7, 1791 from Albany County; boundaries stable throughout the target period.
- Pre-1791 records for this territory fall under Albany County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

**A critical gap shapes all marriage research here.** New York registration history has three phases:

- **1847–c.1849:** Town/city/village clerks were required to register births, marriages, and deaths. Compliance was poor and stopped within a few years. Some Saratoga County town records from this window survive; see the index to births, marriages, and deaths 1848–1850 for Saratoga Springs (online at FamilySearch digital library). (Source: [New York Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records))
- **c.1850–1879:** No operative civil marriage registration at any level. Marriages in this period are documented only in church registers, newspaper notices, or census marriage schedules.
- **1880 onward:** Statewide registration restarted at the town/city level. General compliance for marriages was 1880. Records filed where the event occurred, then copies sent to the state. (Source: [New York Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records))
- **1908 onward:** Saratoga County Clerk began holding county-level marriage records. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Saratoga_County,_New_York_Record_Dates))

**Where held:**
- 1880–1907 town records: individual town and city clerks; Saratoga Springs City Clerk, 474 Broadway, Saratoga Springs, NY 12866
- 1880 onward state index: New York State Marriage Index 1881–1967 at Ancestry (https://search.ancestry.com/search/db.aspx?dbid=61632) — index and images ($); same index free at Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/nymarriageindex)
- 1908+: Saratoga County Clerk, indexed and online at FamilySearch ([New York, County Marriages, 1778–1848; 1908–1937](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1618491)) and Ancestry

**Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (most important), newspaper marriage notices, state census marriage schedules (1865, 1875), naturalization papers.

### Church records

This is the **single most important record category** for an Irish Catholic immigrant marriage in 1855–1879, and an important supplement for 1880–1900. For the core gap years, Catholic parish registers are likely the only surviving record of a marriage.

**Roman Catholic:**
- Saratoga County parishes fall under the **Diocese of Albany**. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- The [Local Catholic Church and Family History Genealogical Research Guide](https://freepages.rootsweb.com/~localcatholic/history/US-NewYorkNY.htm) lists Saratoga County parishes, founding years, and contact information.
- St. Peter's Cemetery in Saratoga Springs is listed on the Saratoga Springs wiki page — indicating a Catholic parish serving Saratoga Springs (the specific parishes should be identified from the Diocese guide above).
- **Notre Dame de Lourdes, Schuylerville:** marriage register June 1889–December 2001. Held at the FamilySearch Library only (not online). FamilySearch Catalog: https://www.familysearch.org/service/search/catalog/item/koha:1054492
- **Findmypast** holds indexed images for [New York Roman Catholic Parish Marriages](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/new-york-roman-catholic-parish-marriages) (subscription) and [New York Catholic Parish Registers Browse](https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/new-york-catholic-parish-registers-browse) (subscription) — these are among the best online sources for Catholic marriages in New York before 1908.
- **Diocese of Albany Archives** is the diocesan repository for deposited parish registers. Contact the Diocese for access.

**Protestant denominations (digitized volumes on FamilySearch):**
- Dutch Reformed, Schuylerville: marriages 1790–1857, 52% name-indexed, also full-text searchable
- First Presbyterian, Ballston Center: marriages 1783–1865, 52% name-indexed, full-text searchable
- Presbyterian, Charlton: marriages 1801–1862, 51% name-indexed, full-text searchable
- Reformed Dutch, Vischer Ferry: marriages 1840–1855, 34% name-indexed, full-text searchable
- Ballston Spa area (multiple volumes, various denominations): 1841–1902, covering marriages 1863–1872, 1872–1882, and 1882–1896 — full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed (must browse image by image); found on FamilySearch
- Methodist Episcopal, Wilton: marriage records 1881–1900 — FamilySearch Library only
- Methodist Episcopal, Schuylerville: 1851–1884 — FamilySearch Library only
- Baptist, Schuylerville: 1835–1869 and 1870–1926 — online at [NYGenWeb](http://saratoganygenweb.com/churchrc.htm)
- Saratoga (town): marriages 1789–1936 in catalog but no images loaded; check FamilySearch Catalog

All church records for this county are in English.

**Digitization summary:** 29 digitized volumes matching marriage/vital/religious categories exist for Saratoga County 1855–1900 on FamilySearch — this is the complete result set. Among the 28 marriage volumes: 11 are browse-only, 10 are full-text searchable but not name-indexed, and several are partially name-indexed (34–52%). None of the identified digitized volumes are specifically Catholic.

### Census records

Census records establish year of marriage, spouse's name, and can suggest when a marriage occurred. The 1865 and 1875 state censuses include marriage schedules.

- **Federal:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900 — indexed, free at FamilySearch; also at Ancestry ($). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed.
- **New York State, 1855:** Indexed and online ([FamilySearch collection 1937366](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1937366), also Ancestry)
- **New York State, 1865:** Indexed and online ([FamilySearch collection 1491284](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1491284)); **includes marriage schedule for the 12 months ending June 1865** — browse to end of population schedule for the relevant town. Marriage entries give husband's name, wife's name, ages, previous marital status, month and day and place of marriage, and church or civil ceremony.
- **New York State, 1875:** Indexed and online ([FamilySearch collection 1918735](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1918735)); **includes marriage schedule for the 12 months ending June 1875** — same browse method.
- **New York State, 1892:** Indexed and online ([FamilySearch collection 1529100](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1529100))

### Probate and court records

Probate records can establish a marriage indirectly by naming spouses, children, and in-laws.
- Saratoga County Surrogate Court holds probate records from 1791; county courthouse, Ballston Spa.
- Online: [New York Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1920234) — browse-only images
- Also: [New York Wills and Probate Records, 1659–1999](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/8800) at Ancestry — index and images ($)
- Divorce papers (from 1847): often state the date and place of the original marriage. Filed with the county Supreme Court; files sealed 100 years.

### Land records

- Survey system: metes and bounds
- Online: [New York Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) — 65.5 million records, index and images
- Saratoga County Clerk holds deed books from 1791

### Military records

For Thomas Hanrahan, born about 1840 in Ireland, Civil War service and pension records are worth checking:
- [New York Civil War Service Records of Union Soldiers, 1861–1865](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1932388) — index and images at FamilySearch
- Pension files at the National Archives (NARA) often name wife, marriage date, and place of marriage
- Town Clerks' Registers of Men Who Served in the Civil War at Ancestry ($); registers exist for most Saratoga County towns

### Cemetery records

- St. Peter's Cemetery (Saratoga Springs): surnames A–Z transcribed online at NYGenWeb (http://saratoganygenweb.com/StPetersA-D.htm)
- Find A Grave and BillionGraves: searchable online for Saratoga County
- [New York Cemetery Abstracts, 1800–1965](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2552111) — index and images at FamilySearch

### Newspaper records

Newspaper marriage notices are among the best substitutes for the 1850–1879 civil record gap.
- [New York Marriage Newspaper Extracts (Barber Collection), 1801–1880](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/8936) at Ancestry — index and images ($)
- [New York Marriage Notices, 1800–1855](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/4244) at Ancestry — index only ($)
- [Index to Marriages and Deaths in the New York Herald, 1856–1863](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/49240) at Ancestry — index ($)
- Saratoga Sentinel index 1819–1837 (Durkee): marriage and death notices, online at Ancestry ($) and FamilySearch catalog
- New York State Historic Newspapers digitization project at http://nyshistoricnewspapers.org/ — search for Saratoga County papers covering the target period

### Immigration/emigration records

An arrival manifest or naturalization paper may give a U.S. address and sometimes marriage information. Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents.
- [New York, County Naturalization Records, 1791–1980](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999177) — index and images at FamilySearch; covers Saratoga County courts
- [New York, Record of Naturalized Voters Registered, 1872–1878](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/4117523) — index and images at FamilySearch
- [New York Passenger Lists, 1820–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1849782) — index and images

### Tax records

- U.S. IRS Tax Assessment Lists, 1862–1918 at Ancestry ($) — can place a person in a specific location between census years
- County property tax records at the Saratoga County Clerk

### Other record types

**City directories:** Saratoga Springs directories are held at the Saratoga Springs Public Library (The Saratoga Room, 49 Henry Street). These can place a family at a specific address between census years.

**Bible records:** New York Family Bible Records, 1581–1917 at Ancestry ($) — may preserve marriage dates recorded in family Bibles.

## Known record losses

No courthouse disasters have been recorded for Saratoga County. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy — Record Loss](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Record_Loss)) The gap in civil marriage records 1849–1879 is a legislative compliance gap, not a physical loss.

## Research tips

- **The 1849–1879 marriage gap:** New York had no operative civil marriage system in this period. For an Irish Catholic couple, search the Catholic parish where they worshipped. The Diocese of Albany guide at https://freepages.rootsweb.com/~localcatholic/history/US-NewYorkNY.htm identifies which parishes existed in Saratoga County and when. Findmypast's New York Roman Catholic Parish Marriages collection (subscription) covers many upstate parishes and is searchable by name. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Church_Records))

- **The 1865 and 1875 state census marriage schedules** are among the best substitutes for a marriage in those specific 12-month windows. Each records husband's and wife's names, ages, marital history, date and place of marriage, and church or civil ceremony. In the FamilySearch images, browse past the end of the population schedule for the relevant town to reach the marriage schedule. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy — Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Census_Records))

- **Town clerk, not county clerk, for 1880–1907 marriages:** Records are filed where the event occurred. For Saratoga Springs, contact the City Clerk. For other towns, contact that town's clerk. The county clerk did not hold marriage records until 1908. (Source: [New York Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records))

- **State marriage index starts 1881:** The New York State Marriage Index 1881–1967 at Ancestry (https://search.ancestry.com/search/db.aspx?dbid=61632) and free at Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/nymarriageindex) covers marriages registered with the state from 1881. This is the first stop if the marriage was after 1880.

- **Naturalization papers can document a marriage indirectly:** Thomas Hanrahan's declaration of intention or final naturalization papers filed in Saratoga County court may give a marriage date, wife's name, or the town where he resided. Search [New York County Naturalization Records, 1791–1980](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999177) on FamilySearch. (Source: [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy — Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy#Naturalization_and_Citizenship))

- **Search neighboring counties:** Albany, Washington, Rensselaer, Warren, Schenectady, Montgomery, and Fulton counties all border Saratoga. If the marriage occurred in any of them, the records will not be in Saratoga County. Albany city Catholic parishes have better-digitized records; an Irish immigrant who married in Albany before moving to Saratoga would appear there, not here. (Source: Neighboring Counties table, [Saratoga County, New York Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy))
